title: Tax systems are balancing household relief, fiscal pressure, investment incentives, and sector-specific extraction
source_unit: OECD Tax Policy Reforms 2026: OECD and Selected Partner Economies
geography: 92 OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework jurisdictions, including all OECD countries

observations.period: Calendar year 2025 reforms introduced or announced; comparative household and public-finance direction

denominator.unit: jurisdictions responding to the OECD annual Tax Policy Reform Questionnaire and covered by the report

policy_objective_pair.value: Tax policy was shaped by supporting growth and investment while responding to mounting budgetary pressures

progressive_pit_direction.value: Revenue-raising personal-income-tax measures were often progressive, including higher top rates and changes to capital-income taxation

cost_of_living_relief.value: Many countries continued base-narrowing measures aimed at supporting low- and middle-income households, though less than in prior years

ssc_direction.value: Social-security-contribution reforms showed a sustained movement toward broader bases and higher rates in several countries

revenue_scope.value: Revenue-raising measures generally remained limited in scope despite public-debt and debt-service pressures

observations.method: OECD comparative review of reforms introduced or announced in 2025, based primarily on the annual questionnaire completed by 92 jurisdictions. The report records stated policy objectives and reform directions; it is not an evaluation of tax incidence, compliance, distribution, or realized revenue.
observations.uncertainty: The report covers announced as well as implemented reforms and notes that it is too early to fully assess some effects. Directional labels such as progressive, base-narrowing, or revenue-raising do not show who ultimately pays, who receives relief, or how behavior changes.
observations.subgroup: Households by income and capital-income exposure, workers and self-employed people, social-protection contributors, national treasuries, and jurisdictions with different fiscal space and demographic pressures.
observations.counterinterpretation: Progressive rate changes can coexist with regressive consumption taxes or reduced public services; household relief can be temporary or poorly targeted; higher contributions can fund social protection rather than simply reduce take-home pay.

observations.period: Calendar year 2025 reforms introduced or announced; firms, platforms, health, and strategic sectors

denominator.unit: jurisdictions in the OECD Corporate Tax Statistics Database for the 2025 combined statutory corporate-income-tax-rate comparison; reform descriptions cover the 92-jurisdiction report universe

average_combined_cit_rate.unit: percent average combined statutory corporate income tax rate across 145 jurisdictions in 2025

average_combined_cit_rate_2000.unit: percent average combined statutory corporate income tax rate across the same database comparison in 2000

corporate_tax_direction.value: Corporate-income-tax base-narrowing measures exceeded base-broadening measures in 2025, commonly citing growth, investment, and innovation

strategic_incentives.value: Countries continued targeted incentives for R&D, emerging technologies, AI, defence, and strategically important sectors

platform_vat.value: More jurisdictions extended VAT collection obligations to non-resident suppliers and online platforms

health_taxes.value: Health-related tax increases, especially tobacco and nicotine excises, were among the most common tax-increasing reform measures

observations.method: OECD comparison of corporate, VAT, health, environmental, and other tax reforms, combining questionnaire responses with the OECD Corporate Tax Statistics Database. The corporate-rate comparison covers 145 jurisdictions while the reform questionnaire covers 92, so the denominators are kept separate.
observations.uncertainty: Statutory rates are not effective tax rates or realized corporate tax payments. Incentives do not establish investment, innovation, employment, or domestic value creation; platform VAT rules do not establish compliance or consumer price incidence; health taxes do not establish behavior or health outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Multinational and domestic firms, online platforms and non-resident suppliers, banks and highly profitable sectors, strategic-technology firms, tobacco/nicotine consumers, and tax administrations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Tax competition and targeted incentives may attract investment or build capability, while base narrowing may reduce public revenue. Platform VAT can improve neutrality without resolving cross-border enforcement or market concentration; health taxes can be fiscal, behavioral, or both.

boundary: This record adds a comparative fiscal-policy route connecting household relief, social contributions, corporate incentives, digital-platform taxation, health taxes, strategic sectors, and public-finance pressure. It does not infer tax incidence, revenue realization, firm investment, household welfare, political legitimacy, or causal behavioral change from reported reform directions.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: OECD Tax Policy Reforms 2026 PDF downloaded from the OECD publication page; jurisdiction coverage, executive-summary reform directions, corporate-rate averages, corporate-base pattern, strategic incentives, platform VAT, and health-tax claims cross-checked against the PDF and OECD release.
